title: Evaluate Agent Behavior with Evidence
summary: Build representative, adversarial, and regression evaluation sets that measure outcomes, trajectories, safety, cost, and latency before agent changes reach production.
objectives: Turn product requirements and failure history into versioned evaluation cases.
Score final outcomes, tool trajectories, policy compliance, cost, and latency with explicit rubrics.
Combine deterministic checks, human review, and model graders without treating any grader as ground truth.
Compare a candidate with a baseline and make a documented release decision.

sections.title: Begin with a claim the evaluation can test
paragraphs: An evaluation is a repeatable experiment, not a demo. Name the workflow version, target population, expected behavior, unacceptable behavior, scoring rule, sample, environment, and release threshold before seeing candidate results. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. Separate task success from style, safety, policy, efficiency, and user experience. A single average can hide a severe regression in one critical slice. code.label: Evaluation case contract
code.code:
caseId: [STABLE ID]
slice: [NORMAL | EDGE | ADVERSARIAL | INCIDENT]
input: [VERSIONED FIXTURE]
expectedOutcome: [OBSERVABLE RESULT]
allowedTrajectory: [TOOLS + BOUNDS]
forbidden: [POLICY OR SAFETY FAILURE]
rubric: [CRITERIA + SCALE + EVIDENCE]
budget: [LATENCY + COST + TURNS]

paragraphs: Use deterministic graders for schema, exact constraints, calculations, tool permissions, postconditions, and latency or cost budgets. sections.title: Compare candidates on identical cases
paragraphs: Run the baseline and candidate against the same versioned cases, environment, budgets, and grader definitions. activity.title: Build and run an agent release evaluation
instructions: Choose one agent workflow and write ten versioned cases: four representative, two boundary, two adversarial, and two prior-failure or incident cases.
Create a 100-point rubric plus deterministic checks for schema, permissions, postconditions, turns, latency, and cost.
Blind-score a baseline and candidate, record grader disagreement, and report results by slice rather than only average.
Make ship, hold, or rollback decisions using thresholds written before the comparison, then add one failed case to the regression set.
evidence: A ten-case evaluation set, 100-point rubric, deterministic grader definitions, and version manifest.
A baseline-versus-candidate report with slice metrics, critical failures, grader disagreement, cost and latency, and a signed release decision.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which aggregate score initially hid the failure that mattered most to the release decision?

questions.prompt: When should release thresholds be defined?
choices: Before running the baseline and candidate comparison
questions.explanation: Predeclared thresholds reduce post-hoc rationalization and make release decisions auditable.

questions.prompt: Why score an agent trajectory as well as its final answer?
choices: A correct answer may have used unsafe tools or exceeded authority
It removes the need for postconditions
questions.explanation: Tool selection, approvals, retries, evidence, and terminal state are part of agent correctness.

questions.prompt: What is the safest role for a model grader?
choices: A calibrated signal compared with deterministic and human evidence
A way to hide rubric changes
questions.explanation: Model graders can be useful but require calibration, versioning, and disagreement review.

questions.prompt: A candidate improves the average but fails a critical permission case. What should the release gate do?
choices: Honor the must-not-regress slice and hold or fix the release
Increase the score weight after the run
questions.explanation: Critical slice gates prevent an aggregate improvement from masking unacceptable harm.

questions.prompt: What makes an evaluation result reproducible?
choices: Versioned cases, fixtures, rubric, graders, workflow configuration, and results
questions.explanation: Every input and decision rule that produced the result must be identifiable.
